Chapter 5: Everyday Practice—Staying Out of the Box in Real Life
You know, the whole challenge of self-deception isn’t something you solve with just one big realization. It’s actually a daily practice, woven right into the little moments of ordinary life.
Every single day, you’ll spot new chances to either slip right back into that old box—or, if you’re paying attention, to step out of it.
Picture this: there’s a parent, doing their best to juggle work and family, and one evening they find themselves snapping at their kid for forgetting a simple chore. The old story kicks in—maybe it sounds familiar? “They never listen,” or “I do everything around here.” But this time, the parent catches themselves.
They pause, take a breath, and suddenly remember—their child’s probably tired too, maybe even overwhelmed with schoolwork. So, the conversation shifts. Instead of accusing, they lean in with understanding. That moment passes, but what sticks around is the feeling of connection.
Or think about a teammate who’s frustrated by a colleague who keeps asking questions. It’s so tempting in that split second to roll your eyes and see them as nothing but a nuisance. But instead, you decide to help out—maybe because you remember times when you needed someone’s support.
The interaction’s over in a few minutes, but both of you walk away feeling respected.
These aren’t dramatic moments, but they really count. Each time you choose to see someone else as a person—not just an obstacle or annoyance—you’re building a new habit.
And bit by bit, it gets easier to notice when you’re slipping back into the box, to pause, and to make a different choice.
Now, staying out of the box doesn’t mean you ignore problems or pretend to like everyone. Not at all. It’s about showing up to each situation with curiosity and humility—being open to see beyond just your own view.
It means remembering that everyone around you has their own battles, and often, kindness is the best possible response.
And here’s something important—it’s not just for leaders or managers. This practice is for anyone who wants better relationships—whether that’s at work, at home, or out in the community.
It’s about taking ownership of your own mindset, and trusting that even small changes can make a big difference.
The truth is, this journey never really ends. There’ll be setbacks—days when frustration gets the better of you, or when that box feels impossible to escape. But every new day brings another chance.
Another chance to see the people around you more clearly, to try again, and to slowly build the kind of relationships that make life—and work—feel more meaningful.
